issues.what: The title, subtitle, note, and “longer left tail” annotation identify the curve as left-skewed, but the parameters specify a right-skewed chi-square distribution with 4 degrees of freedom.
issues.why: This distribution peaks at x = 2, has a short left side bounded by zero, and a long tail toward larger values. It therefore illustrates right skew, not left skew.

issues.what: The alt text describes a long tail stretching left toward smaller values.
issues.why: The specified curve’s long tail stretches right. The alt text also contradicts itself by describing the left side as both a long tail and a steep drop to zero.

issues.what: The curve plotted is skewed right, but the labels and title describe it as skewed left.
issues.why: A chi-square distribution with 4 degrees of freedom is skewed to the right (it has a long right tail). However, the title ('Skewed left'), subtitle, alt text, and the text label 'longer left tail' (placed at x=11.5, which is on the right side of the distribution) all incorrectly claim that the distribution is skewed left. This would severely confuse a student about the definition of skewness.

issues.what: The mean and median labels are reversed, and the alt text repeats the reversal.
issues.why: For a chi-square distribution with 4 degrees of freedom, the mean is 4.0 and the median is approximately 3.356. The left line is therefore the median and the right line is the mean, contrary to the figure’s labels and alt text. This also contradicts the title and note stating that the mean is larger than the median.

issues.what: The labels and alt text swap the mean and median, incorrectly stating that the mean is smaller than the median.
issues.why: For a chi-square distribution with df = 4, the mean is 4.0 and the median is approximately 3.36. Thus, the mean is the right line (4.0) and the median is the left line (3.36). The figure's text labels ('mean (left line)' and 'median (right line)') and the alt text ('the mean is the left line... so the mean is smaller than the median') are incorrect and contradict the title 'Skewed right: the mean is above the median'.

issues.what: The subtitle and alt text say the long left tail pulls the mean toward larger values.
issues.why: A long left tail pulls the mean toward smaller values, consistent with the plotted mean of 12.0 being below the median of 12.644.

issues.what: The alt text concludes that the mean is larger than the median, and the note says this is usual for left-skewed distributions.
issues.why: The plotted values show 12.0 < 12.644. Both statements reverse the relationship shown and contradict the entry's claim that the mean is usually smaller than the median under left skew.
The subtitle states 'The long left tail pulls the mean toward larger values', but a left tail pulls the mean toward smaller values (to the left).
The alt text states 'The mean is the left line, at about 12.0, and the median is the right line, at about 12.6, so the mean is larger than the median.' 12.0 is smaller than 12.6, not larger.
The note states 'In a left-skewed distribution the mean is usually larger than the median.' This is incorrect; in a left-skewed distribution, the mean is usually smaller than the median.

issues.what: The title labels the distribution “skewed right,” but the curve is skewed left.
issues.why: The mirrored chi-square curve has a longer tail toward smaller values, as the subtitle and skew check confirm. Skew direction is named by the longer tail, not the peak.

issues.what: The alt text and note teach that skew is named for the side containing the peak or most of the data.
issues.why: That rule is false and contradicts the entry’s claim. A peak on the right with a long left tail indicates left (negative) skew.

issues.what: The figure title, subtitle, alt text, and note incorrectly define skewness direction.
issues.why: The figure claims that a distribution with a peak on the right and a long tail to the left is 'skewed right' and that skew is named for the peak/where most data are. In reality, skew is named for the tail: a long tail to the left (smaller values) is skewed left, which also contradicts the authored reference entry's definition.

issues.what: The alt text says the mean is much larger than the median and that they are far apart.
issues.why: The normal distribution has mean and median both equal to 8, consistent with the single line labelled “mean = median.”

issues.what: The note states that in a symmetric distribution the mean is usually much larger than the median.
issues.why: For the symmetric normal distribution shown, the mean and median are equal. The note also contradicts the entry’s claim that they are close under relative symmetry.

issues.what: The note states: 'In a symmetric distribution the mean is usually much larger than the median.'
issues.why: This is factually incorrect. In a symmetric distribution, the mean and median are approximately equal (or exactly equal if perfectly symmetric).

issues.what: The alt text states: 'The mean is much larger than the median, so they are far apart.'
issues.why: This contradicts the figure itself (which shows a symmetric normal distribution with a single line labeled 'mean = median' at 8.0) and the scientific reality of symmetric distributions.
